mainTopic: The exemptions of an אונן and of one who guards the dead, and the honor owed to the dead: escorting them, carrying their bones, and not mocking them in a בית הקברות
overview: This amud finishes a ברייתא about an אונן, a mourner whose relative is not yet buried. On a weekday he is exempt from קריאת שמע, תפלה, תפילין and all מצוות, but on שבת he eats normally and is obligated in everything. רבי יוחנן explains that רבן שמעון בן גמליאל differs from the תנא קמא about תשמיש המטה. The גמרא then asks how the ברייתא fits the משנה's words "מתו מוטל לפניו". רב פפא limits the ברייתא to eating in the same room, and רב אשי says the duty to bury counts as "before him," bringing a proof from אברהם. Next the גמרא shows that a guard of any body is also exempt, while someone walking in a בית הקברות is affected only within ארבע אמות of a grave. A ברייתא teaches that two guards take turns, and בן עזאי lets both pray on a boat; רבינא explains that they disagree about worrying over mice. Then come teachings on respect for bones and a ספר תורה while travelling, and on the duty and reward of escorting the dead. The amud ends with the story of רבי חייא and רבי יונתן in a בית הקברות and the proof that צדיקים are called "living" even after death, which continues on the next amud.

steps.title: On a weekday the mourner is exempt from blessings and מצוות
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא continues: an אונן is not included by others in ברכות or זימון. He is also exempt from קריאת שמע, תפלה, תפילין and all מצוות of the תורה.
steps.simpleTranslation: Others do not say a ברכה for him, and others do not include him in a זימון. He is exempt from קריאת שמע, from תפלה, from תפילין, and from all the מצוות stated in the תורה.
steps.whatsHappening: We are in the middle of a ברייתא that began on the previous page. It lists everything an אונן does not do on a regular weekday.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Earlier in the ברייתא it said he eats in another room and does not make his own ברכה. Here it adds two things. First, others cannot say a ברכה for him or count him for a זימון. Second, he is exempt from all positive מצוות, because his duty to bury the dead takes priority.

keyTerms.meaning: A mourner whose close relative has died but is not yet buried
Making a זימון, the group invitation to ברכת המזון for three or more people
Others say a ברכה on his behalf

phrases.english: And they do not recite a blessing on his behalf,
phrases.notes: Others cannot make the ברכה for him to fulfill his obligation.

phrases.english: and they do not invite him to a zimun,
phrases.notes: He is not counted toward the three needed for זימון.

phrases.english: and he is exempt from reciting Shema
and from prayer and from tefillin
and from all the מצוות stated in the Torah.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאֵין מְבָרְכִין עָלָיו
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the ברייתא begun on the previous daf (17b).
steps.mimraCoreRuling: On a weekday an אונן is exempt from all מצוות and is not counted for ברכות or זימון.

steps.title: On Shabbat the mourner eats normally and keeps all מצוות
steps.stepSummary: On שבת the אונן reclines, eats meat, drinks wine and makes ברכות and זימון. Others may also include him, and he is obligated in all מצוות.
steps.simpleTranslation: On שבת he reclines and eats meat and drinks wine. He blesses and leads a זימון, others bless for him and include him in a זימון, and he is obligated in all the מצוות stated in the תורה.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא now switches to שבת. It reverses everything it just said about the weekday.
steps.deeperAnalysis: On שבת he cannot bury the dead, so he has no burial duty that pushes away other מצוות. Also, there is no public mourning on שבת. So he eats a normal שבת meal and returns to full obligation.

keyTerms.meaning: Reclines, the normal way of eating a formal meal

phrases.english: And on Shabbat he reclines and eats meat
and drinks wine,
and he blesses and leads a zimun,
and others bless on his behalf and include him in a zimun,
and he is obligated in all the מצוות
stated in the Torah.

steps.triggerLanguage: וּבְשַׁבָּת מֵיסֵב וְאוֹכֵל בָּשָׂר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Contrasts the שבת law with the weekday law in step 1.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: On שבת an אונן eats normally and is obligated in all מצוות.

steps.title: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל: obligated in these, so obligated in all
steps.stepSummary: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל says that since the אונן is obligated in these שבת practices, he is obligated in all מצוות.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל says: Since he became obligated in these, he became obligated in all of them.
steps.whatsHappening: A second תנא gives his view about the אונן on שבת.
steps.deeperAnalysis: His words sound almost the same as the תנא קמא, who also said he is obligated in all מצוות on שבת. This sameness sets up the next step, where the גמרא asks what the actual difference between them is.

keyTerms.meaning: A תנא who disagrees with the first opinion

phrases.english: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says:
Since he became obligated in these,
phrases.notes: "These" are the שבת meal practices just listed.

phrases.english: he became obligated in all of them.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבָּן שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן גַּמְלִיאֵל אוֹמֵר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second opinion that seems to say the same as the תנא קמא.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Obligation in the שבת practices brings obligation in every מצוה.

steps.title: רבי יוחנן: the dispute is about תשמיש המטה
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן asks what the difference is between the two opinions. He answers that they argue about תשמיש המטה on שבת.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבי יוחנן said: What is the difference between them? תשמיש המטה is the difference between them.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוחנן asks what the practical difference is between the תנא קמא and רבן שמעון בן גמליאל, and then he answers it himself.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both opinions say the אונן is obligated in מצוות on שבת, so a real difference must exist. The תנא קמא forbids תשמיש המטה, because holding back from it is private and is not a public sign of mourning. רבן שמעון בן גמליאל's word "all" includes even this מצוה, so he requires it.

keyTerms.meaning: What is the difference between them?
There is a difference between them
An אמורא who explains the dispute

phrases.english: And Rabbi Yochanan said:
What is the difference between them?
Marital relations is the difference between them.

steps.triggerLanguage: מַאי בֵּינַיְיהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains how step 3 actually differs from step 2.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The תנא קמא forbids תשמיש המטה for an אונן on שבת, and רבן שמעון בן גמליאל requires it.

steps.title: The ברייתא exempts him even when the dead is in another room
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא points out that the ברייתא exempts the אונן from all מצוות even when he eats in another house. This seems to clash with the משנה, which speaks only of the dead lying before him.
steps.simpleTranslation: In any case, it teaches that he is exempt from קריאת שמע, from תפלה, from תפילין, and from all the מצוות stated in the תורה!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to the weekday part of the ברייתא and raises a problem with it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה says "מי שמתו מוטל לפניו" is exempt, which suggests he is exempt only when the body is physically in front of him. The ברייתא, however, places him in another house and still exempts him. So the two sources seem to disagree.

keyTerms.meaning: In any case, it teaches. The גמרא uses this to pull out the relevant point from a source.
His dead lies before him (the משנה's wording)

steps.confusionAlert: The question is not about the שבת part or about רבי יוחנן's point. It goes back to the weekday exemption in step 1 and compares it to the משנה's words "before him."

phrases.english: In any case, it teaches:
he is exempt from reciting Shema and from prayer
and from tefillin
and from all the מצוות stated in the Torah!

steps.triggerLanguage: קָתָנֵי מִיהַת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Returns to the weekday exemption of step 1 and checks it against the משנה.
steps.kashyaTarget: The משנה's limit of "מתו מוטל לפניו"
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא exempts him even when he is in another house, but the משנה implies he is exempt only when the dead is literally in front of him.

steps.title: רב פפא: the exemption refers to eating in the same room
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא says that the ברייתא's exemption refers only to the case where he has no other room and eats with his face turned away. In that case the dead really is before him.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפא said: Explain it as referring to the case where he turns his face away and eats.
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא answers the question by limiting which case the exemption is talking about.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא lists several cases: he eats in another house, or in a friend's house, or he turns his face away. רב פפא attaches the exemption only to the last case, where the body is physically present. So the ברייתא and the משנה agree that the exemption applies only when the dead is literally in front of him.

phrases.english: Rav Pappa said:
Explain it as referring to one who turns his face away and eats.
phrases.notes: אַמַּחֲזִיר is a contraction of עַל מַחֲזִיר, meaning "on the case of one who turns."

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב פָּפָּא תַּרְגְּמָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא in step 5.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limiting the ruling to a specific case
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The exemption applies to every case in the ברייתא, even another house.
steps.terutzMaskana: The exemption applies only when he eats in the same room as the dead.

steps.title: רב אשי: the duty to bury counts as "before him"
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי says that as long as the burial is his responsibility, it is as if the dead lies before him, even when he is in another room.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אשי said: Since it is upon him to bury him, it is as if the dead lies before him.
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי gives a second answer to the same question. He changes how we read the משנה, not the ברייתא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב פפא read "before him" in the משנה physically and limited the ברייתא. רב אשי instead reads "before him" as "his responsibility." So the ברייתא's exemption covers every case, including another house, and there is no conflict with the משנה.

keyTerms.meaning: It is placed upon him, it is his duty

phrases.english: Rav Ashi said:
Since it is incumbent upon him to bury him,
it is considered as if he lies before him.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב אָשֵׁי אָמַר כֵּיוָן שֶׁמּוּטָּל עָלָיו לְקוֹבְרוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second answer to step 5, different from רב פפא's answer.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redefining a term in the משנה
steps.terutzHavaAmina: "Before him" means physically in front of him.
steps.terutzMaskana: "Before him" means that the burial is still his responsibility, wherever he is.

steps.title: Proof from אברהם: "bury my dead from before me"
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי brings פסוקים about אברהם. אברהם had already left the body, yet he still called it "before me," because he still had to bury it.
steps.simpleTranslation: As it says: "And אברהם rose from before his dead," and it says: "So that I may bury my dead from before me." As long as it is upon him to bury him, it is as if he lies before him.
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי supports his reading of "before him" with two פסוקים from בראשית.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first פסוק shows that אברהם got up and left the body of שרה. Yet in the next פסוק, while away from her, he still says "מלפני," from before me. This shows that "before me" can describe a body one is responsible to bury, not only one that is physically present.

keyTerms.meaning: As it is said in a פסוק
So that I may bury my dead from before me (בראשית כ"ג:ד)

steps.whatToRemember: There are two ways to read "מתו מוטל לפניו." רב פפא reads it as physically in front of him. רב אשי reads it as the burial still being his responsibility, which he learns from אברהם.

phrases.english: As it is stated:
"And Abraham rose up from before his dead,"
phrases.notes: He had already left the body.

phrases.english: and it is stated:
"So that I may bury my dead from before me,"
As long as it is incumbent upon him to bury him,
it is considered as if he lies before him.

steps.triggerLanguage: שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר וַיָּקׇם אַבְרָהָם מֵעַל פְּנֵי מֵתוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the source for רב אשי's answer in step 7.
steps.raayaObject: רב אשי's claim that the duty to bury counts as "before him"
steps.raayaSupportSource: בראשית כ"ג:ג-ד, where אברהם speaks of his dead as "before me" even after leaving her

steps.title: Only one's own dead, not one who is just guarding
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא infers that the exemption applies to "his dead," a relative he must bury. Someone who is only guarding a body is not exempt by this rule.
steps.simpleTranslation: His dead: yes. But one who guards him: no.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא draws an inference from the word "מתו," his dead. This sets up the next discussion, which is about someone guarding a body.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The exemption is tied to the personal duty to bury, which belongs to a relative. A person who only watches over a body has no such duty. So this exemption does not apply to him. The next lines will ask whether a guard has some other reason to be exempt.

phrases.english: His dead: yes,
but one who guards him: no.

steps.triggerLanguage: מֵתוֹ אִין אֲבָל מְשַׁמְּרוֹ לָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws a limit from the word "מתו" and opens a new topic about one who guards a body.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The exemption applies to a relative with the duty to bury, not to someone who only guards the body.

steps.title: A ברייתא exempts even someone guarding a body that is not his relative
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the inference from Step 9 by quoting a ברייתא that exempts anyone who guards a dead body, even if it is not his relative.
steps.simpleTranslation: But wasn't it taught in a ברייתא: One who guards a dead body, even though it is not his own dead relative, is exempt from קריאת שמע, from תפילה, from תפילין, and from all the מצוות stated in the תורה!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא just said that only 'his dead' (a relative) creates an exemption. Now it brings a ברייתא that seems to say the opposite: even a guard of a stranger's body is exempt.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 9 suggested that a person who only guards a body is not exempt. This ברייתא openly says that such a guard IS exempt from all מצוות. So the inference seems to be contradicted by a direct source.

keyTerms.meaning: But wasn't it taught in a ברייתא? (opening of a challenge)
One who guards the dead body
His own dead, a relative he must bury

phrases.english: But wasn't it taught: One who guards the dead,
even though it is not his own dead relative —
is exempt from reciting Shema and from prayer
and from tefillin
and from all the מצוות stated in the Torah!

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהָתַנְיָא: הַמְשַׁמֵּר אֶת הַמֵּת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the inference made in Step 9
steps.kashyaTarget: The inference that only 'his dead' exempts, and that a mere guard is not exempt
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A ברייתא explicitly exempts a guard even when the body is not his relative

steps.title: Both the guard and the relative are exempt
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that there is no contradiction: the guard is exempt even if it is not his relative, and the relative is exempt even if he is not guarding.
steps.simpleTranslation: The one guarding it is exempt even though it is not his relative, and the relative is exempt even though he is not guarding it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains that the two sources fit together. Each one teaches a different reason for being exempt.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 9 had inferred from the word "מתו" that a guard is not exempt. The גמרא now drops that inference and reads the משנה and the ברייתא as complementary. There are two separate reasons for exemption: guarding the body, or being the relative responsible to bury it.
steps.whatToRemember: There are two separate reasons for exemption: (1) guarding any body, and (2) being the relative who must bury it, even when he is not guarding.

phrases.aramaic: מְשַׁמְּרוֹ, אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁאֵינוֹ מֵתוֹ,
phrases.english: One who guards it is exempt, even though it is not his dead relative;

phrases.aramaic: מֵתוֹ אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁאֵינוֹ מְשַׁמְּרוֹ.
phrases.english: one whose dead relative it is is exempt, even though he is not guarding it.

steps.triggerLanguage: מְשַׁמְּרוֹ, אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁאֵינוֹ מֵתוֹ, מֵתוֹ אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁאֵינוֹ מְשַׁמְּרוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Resolves the challenge of Step 10
steps.terutzResolutionType: Harmonization: the two sources describe two separate grounds for exemption
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Only the relative is exempt; a guard of a stranger's body is not
steps.terutzMaskana: Both the guard and the relative are exempt, each for his own reason

steps.title: What about someone walking in a cemetery?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא infers that only the relative or the guard is exempt, not someone walking in a בית הקברות. Then it challenges this with a ברייתא that forbids wearing תפילין and reading Torah in a cemetery.
steps.simpleTranslation: His relative, or one who guards — yes, they are exempt. But one who walks in a בית הקברות — no, he is not. But wasn't it taught: A person should not walk in a בית הקברות with תפילין on his head and a ספר תורה on his arm while reading from it. If he does so, he transgresses the פסוק 'One who mocks the poor insults his Maker.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא concludes that only the relative and the guard are exempt, which implies that a person just walking in a בית הקברות is still obligated. It then brings a ברייתא that seems to show that he cannot do מצוות there.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If a person walking in a cemetery were obligated in מצוות, he should be allowed to wear תפילין and read Torah. Yet the ברייתא forbids it, because doing מצוות in front of the dead mocks them, since they can no longer do מצוות. So the person walking there seems to be exempt too.

keyTerms.meaning: Mocking the poor (here: the dead, who cannot do מצוות)

phrases.english: His dead relative, or one guarding it — yes, exempt;
but one walking in a cemetery — no, not exempt.

phrases.aramaic: וְהָתַנְיָא: לֹא יְהַלֵּךְ אָדָם בְּבֵית הַקְּבָרוֹת
phrases.english: But wasn't it taught: A person may not walk in a cemetery
with tefillin on his head
and a Torah scroll on his arm, reading from it.
And if he does so —
he transgresses because of 'One who mocks the poor insults his Maker.'
phrases.notes: משלי יז:ה. The dead are 'poor' because they can no longer do מצוות.

steps.triggerLanguage: מֵתוֹ וּמְשַׁמְּרוֹ — אִין, אֲבָל מְהַלֵּךְ בְּבֵית הַקְּבָרוֹת — לָא. וְהָתַנְיָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws an inference from Step 11's conclusion and challenges it
steps.kashyaTarget: The implication that a person walking in a cemetery is obligated in מצוות
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A ברייתא forbids תפילין and Torah reading in a cemetery, so it seems such a person cannot do מצוות there either

steps.title: In the cemetery only four אמות around a grave count; the relative and the guard are exempt even beyond that
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that in a cemetery the prohibition applies only within ארבע אמות of a grave, and beyond that he is obligated. The relative and the guard are exempt even beyond ארבע אמות.
steps.simpleTranslation: There, in the cemetery, it is forbidden only within four אמות, and beyond four אמות he is obligated. As the Master said: a dead body 'occupies' four אמות with regard to קריאת שמע. Here, with the relative or the guard, he is exempt even beyond four אמות.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains the difference between the two cases. The difference is a matter of distance.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A person walking in a cemetery is affected only when he is close to a grave, within ארבע אמות. Outside that area he is fully obligated, so the inference from Step 12 still holds. The relative and the guard are different: their exemption does not depend on distance at all.

keyTerms.meaning: Four cubits, the space a dead body is considered to 'occupy'
As the Master said (quoting an accepted teaching)

steps.confusionAlert: Do not think the person walking in the cemetery is exempt everywhere there. He is affected only within ארבע אמות of a grave. The relative and the guard are exempt no matter how far away they are.

phrases.aramaic: הָתָם, תּוֹךְ אַרְבַּע אַמּוֹת הוּא דְאָסוּר,
phrases.english: There, it is only within four cubits that it is forbidden;
beyond four cubits — he is obligated.
As the Master said:

phrases.aramaic: מֵת תּוֹפֵס אַרְבַּע אַמּוֹת לִקְרִיאַת שְׁמַע.
phrases.english: A dead body occupies four cubits with regard to reciting Shema.

phrases.aramaic: הָכָא, חוּץ לְאַרְבַּע אַמּוֹת נָמֵי פָּטוּר.
phrases.english: Here, even beyond four cubits he is also exempt.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָתָם, תּוֹךְ אַרְבַּע אַמּוֹת הוּא דְאָסוּר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Resolves the challenge of Step 12
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinction by distance (within or beyond four אמות)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The person walking in a cemetery seems to be exempt like the relative and the guard
steps.terutzMaskana: The cemetery walker is affected only within four אמות; the relative and the guard are exempt even beyond them
steps.whyThisMatters: This sets up the practical rule of ארבע אמות around a dead body or grave for קריאת שמע and other מצוות.

steps.title: Returning to the guarding ברייתא itself
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא says 'גופא' and quotes the guarding ברייתא again, so that it can study the rest of it.
steps.simpleTranslation: Returning to the matter itself: One who guards a dead body, even though it is not his relative, is exempt from קריאת שמע, from תפילה, from תפילין, and from all the מצוות stated in the תורה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is setting up its next move. It goes back to the ברייתא quoted in Step 10 in order to study the rest of it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Up to now, the ברייתא was quoted only as a challenge. Now the גמרא repeats its first line as a starting point for analyzing its next parts, which deal with how guards can still do מצוות.

keyTerms.meaning: 'The matter itself': returning to study a source that was quoted earlier

phrases.english: Returning to the matter itself.

phrases.aramaic: הַמְשַׁמֵּר אֶת הַמֵּת אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁאֵינוֹ מֵתוֹ —
phrases.english: One who guards the dead, even though it is not his dead relative —

phrases.aramaic: פָּטוּר מִקְּרִיאַת שְׁמַע וּמִן הַתְּפִלָּה וּמִן הַתְּפִילִּין
phrases.english: is exempt from reciting Shema, from prayer, and from tefillin
and from all the מצוות stated in the Torah.

steps.triggerLanguage: גּוּפָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the challenge cycle and returns to analyze the ברייתא from Step 10
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A guard of any dead body is exempt from all מצוות

steps.title: Two guards take turns
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא continues: if there are two guards, they take turns, so that one guards while the other reads קריאת שמע.
steps.simpleTranslation: If there were two guards, this one guards while that one reads, and then that one guards while this one reads.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא teaches that when there are two guards, the exemption does not apply to both at the same time. They must take turns so that each one can do the מצוה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The guard is exempt only because the job of guarding keeps him busy. If someone else can guard, he is free and therefore obligated. So two guards must take turns reading.

keyTerms.meaning: This one guards and that one reads

phrases.english: If there were two —
this one guards and that one reads,
and then that one guards and this one reads.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָיוּ שְׁנַיִם — זֶה מְשַׁמֵּר וְזֶה קוֹרֵא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the ברייתא with a limit on the guard's exemption
steps.mimraCoreRuling: With two guards, they alternate so that each one recites קריאת שמע

steps.title: בן עזאי: on a boat, both can pray together
steps.stepSummary: בן עזאי says that if they are travelling on a boat, they may put the body in one corner and both pray in another corner.
steps.simpleTranslation: בן עזאי says: If they were travelling on a boat, he places the body in this corner, and both of them pray in another corner.
steps.whatsHappening: בן עזאי adds a case where the guards do not need to take turns. On a boat, both may pray at once.
steps.deeperAnalysis: On a boat the body is safe from wild animals, so בן עזאי holds it does not really need active guarding. Because of that, both people may leave it in one corner and pray together in another corner.
steps.whatToRemember: The guard's exemption depends on whether guarding is really needed. According to בן עזאי, when it is not needed, as on a boat, both people may pray; the תנא קמא disagrees (see step 18).

phrases.english: Ben Azzai says:
If they were travelling on a boat —
he places it in this corner,
and both of them pray in another corner.

steps.triggerLanguage: בֶּן עַזַּאי אוֹמֵר: הָיוּ בָּאִים בִּסְפִינָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds another opinion and case to the ברייתא's rule about guards
steps.mimraCoreRuling: On a boat, the body may be set aside and both may pray together

steps.title: What is the difference between the two opinions?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what practical difference there is between the תנא קמא and בן עזאי in the boat case.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the difference between them?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a short question to set up the next step. In practice, how do the two opinions about the guards and the boat differ?
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא says two guards must take turns. בן עזאי says that on a boat both may leave the body in a corner and go pray. The גמרא wants to know what real-life point they disagree about.

keyTerms.meaning: What is the difference between them? (asks for the practical difference between two opinions)

phrases.english: What is the difference between them?

steps.triggerLanguage: מַאי בֵּינַיְיהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks about the dispute between the ברייתא (Step 15) and בן עזאי (Step 16).
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The practical point of disagreement between the תנא קמא and בן עזאי.

steps.title: They disagree about worrying over mice
steps.stepSummary: רבינא explains that the dispute is whether we worry that mice might harm the body, even on a boat.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבינא said: The difference between them is whether we worry about mice. One Sage holds that we worry. The other Sage holds that we do not worry.
steps.whatsHappening: רבינא answers the question. The two opinions disagree about whether mice could reach and damage an unguarded body on a boat.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The תנא קמא worries about mice everywhere, even on a boat, so one guard must always stay with the body. בן עזאי holds there is no such worry on a boat, so both guards may leave the body in a corner and pray. In both opinions the body still needs protection from animals; they only disagree about whether that danger exists on a boat.

keyTerms.meaning: An אמורא who gives the answer

steps.confusionAlert: Both opinions agree that a body may not be left where animals could harm it. They disagree only about whether that danger exists on a boat.

phrases.english: Ravina said:
Concern about mice is the difference between them.
One Sage holds: we are concerned.
phrases.notes: The תנא קמא, who requires one guard to stay.

phrases.english: And the other Sage holds: we are not concerned.
phrases.notes: בן עזאי, who allows both to pray on the boat.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רָבִינָא: חוֹשְׁשִׁין לְעַכְבָּרִים אִיכָּא בֵּינַיְיהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of Step 17.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The dispute is whether we worry that mice will harm the body on a boat.

steps.title: Do not ride on bones you are carrying, unless you are in danger
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא teaches that carrying bones in a saddlebag and riding on them is disrespectful and forbidden, but allowed in danger. The same applies to a ספר תורה.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Rabbis taught: Someone carrying bones from place to place should not put them in a saddlebag, place them on a donkey, and ride on them, because that treats them disrespectfully. If he is afraid of gentiles or bandits, it is permitted. And just as they said about bones, so they said about a ספר תורה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new ברייתא about honoring the remains of the dead. It forbids sitting on bones while travelling, except when there is danger.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Sitting on bones uses them like ordinary luggage, which is a disgrace. When there is danger from gentiles or bandits, he must travel quickly, so the rule is relaxed. The last line adds that a ספר תורה follows the same rules, which sets up the next question.

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught:
One who carries bones from place to place,
he should not put them in a saddlebag
and put them on a donkey's back
and ride on them,
because he treats them disrespectfully.
But if he was afraid of gentiles
or of bandits, it is permitted.
And just as they said about bones,
so they said about a Torah scroll.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: הַמּוֹלִיךְ עֲצָמוֹת מִמָּקוֹם לְמָקוֹם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves to a new ברייתא on the related theme of respect for the dead.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Riding on bones is forbidden as a disgrace but permitted in danger, and the same applies to a ספר תורה.

steps.title: Which part does the ספר תורה line refer to?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks which clause of the ברייתא the comparison to a ספר תורה refers to.
steps.simpleTranslation: To which part?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a short setup question. Does the ספר תורה line refer to the first part (the prohibition) or to the second part (the danger leniency)?
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא has two parts: a ban on riding on bones, and a permission when there is danger. The words 'just as they said' could point to either part, so the גמרא needs to clarify.

keyTerms.meaning: To which one? (which clause is meant)

phrases.english: To which part does it refer?

steps.triggerLanguage: אַהֵיָיא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions the last line of the ברייתא in Step 19.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether the ספר תורה comparison refers to the first clause or the latter clause.

steps.title: The first clause would be obvious for a ספר תורה
steps.stepSummary: If the comparison referred to the first clause, it would be obvious. A ספר תורה is surely no less holy than bones.
steps.simpleTranslation: If you say it refers to the first part, that is obvious! Is a ספר תורה less important than bones?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tests the first possibility and rejects it. The ברייתא would not need to teach something so obvious.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Of course one may not ride on a ספר תורה if one may not even ride on bones. A ברייתא does not teach what is self-evident, so the first clause cannot be what is meant.

phrases.english: If you say it refers to the first clause, that is obvious!
Is a Torah scroll any less than bones?

steps.triggerLanguage: אִילֵּימָא אַרֵישָׁא — פְּשִׁיטָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Tests and rejects the first option raised in Step 20.
steps.kashyaTarget: The reading that the ספר תורה line refers to the prohibition clause.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: That reading makes the line obvious (פשיטא), since a ספר תורה is surely no less holy than bones.

steps.title: It refers to the danger leniency
steps.stepSummary: The comparison must refer to the latter clause: in danger, one may ride on a ספר תורה too.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, it refers to the latter part.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא concludes that the ספר תורה line refers to the danger leniency.
steps.deeperAnalysis: One might have thought a ספר תורה is so holy that one may never sit on it, even in danger. The ברייתא teaches that saving one's life overrides this, just as it does for bones.
steps.whatToRemember: The ספר תורה line teaches a leniency: in danger, one may ride on it, just as with bones.

phrases.english: Rather, it refers to the latter clause.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא אַסֵּיפָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Resolves the question after the first option was rejected in Step 21.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reassigns the line to a different clause
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The line might refer to the prohibition, which would be obvious.
steps.terutzMaskana: It refers to the danger leniency, which applies even to a ספר תורה.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The ספר תורה comparison refers to the latter clause: in danger one may ride on a ספר תורה, just as with bones.

steps.title: Ignoring a funeral mocks the Creator
steps.stepSummary: רחבה quotes רב יהודה: someone who sees a funeral and does not escort the dead transgresses 'לעג לרש חרף עשהו'.
steps.simpleTranslation: רחבה said in the name of רב יהודה: Anyone who sees a dead person being carried and does not escort him transgresses the verse 'One who mocks the poor insults his Maker.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new teaching about the duty to escort the dead (לוויית המת).
steps.deeperAnalysis: The dead person is the 'poor one' (רש), because he can no longer do any מצוות. Ignoring him is like mocking him, and that insults ה׳ who created him.

keyTerms.meaning: An אמורא who passes on the teaching
One who mocks the poor insults his Maker (משלי יז:ה)

steps.whyThisMatters: This is a source for the obligation of לוויית המת when one sees a funeral.

phrases.english: Rachava said that Rav Yehuda said:
Anyone who sees the dead and does not escort him
transgresses because of 'One who mocks the poor insults his Maker.'

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַחֲבָה אָמַר רַב יְהוּדָה: כָּל הָרוֹאֶה הַמֵּת וְאֵינוֹ מְלַוֵּהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new teaching on the broader theme of honoring the dead.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Not escorting a funeral one sees is a sin of mocking the poor.

steps.title: What is the reward for escorting the dead?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what reward a person receives if he does escort the dead.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if he did escort him, what is his reward?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a question that sets up the next statement. We know the punishment for not escorting, so what is the reward for escorting?
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 23 gave the negative side. Now the גמרא asks about the positive side, which רב אסי will answer.

phrases.english: And if he escorted him, what is his reward?

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִם הִלְוָהוּ מַה שְּׂכָרוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Follows up on Step 23 by asking about the reward.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The reward for escorting the dead.

steps.title: Escorting the dead is like lending to ה׳
steps.stepSummary: רב אסי applies two verses: one who helps the poor lends to ה׳, and one who is kind to the needy honors Him.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אסי said: About him the verse says, 'One who is kind to the poor lends to ה׳,' and 'One who is gracious to the needy honors Him.'
steps.whatsHappening: רב אסי answers the question with verses from משלי. Escorting the dead is a great kindness that ה׳ repays.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The dead person is the 'poor one' who cannot repay. ה׳ treats the kindness as a loan to Himself, and the end of that פסוק (וּגְמֻלוֹ יְשַׁלֶּם לוֹ, which is not quoted here) promises repayment. The second verse adds that this kindness honors ה׳, the opposite of 'insulting his Maker.'

keyTerms.meaning: One who is kind to the poor lends to ה׳‎ (משלי יט:יז)
One who is gracious to the needy honors Him (משלי יד:לא)

steps.whatToRemember: Not escorting the dead insults ה׳; escorting the dead honors ה׳ and is repaid like a loan.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב אַסִּי, עָלָיו הַכָּתוּב אוֹמֵר:
phrases.english: Rav Asi said: About him the verse says:
'He who is kind to the poor lends to the Lord'
'and he who is gracious to the needy honors Him.'

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב אַסִּי, עָלָיו הַכָּתוּב אוֹמֵר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of Step 24.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Escorting the dead counts as lending to ה׳ and honoring Him, and ה׳ repays it.

steps.title: רבי חייא tells רבי יונתן to lift his ציצית in the בית הקברות
steps.stepSummary: רבי חייא and רבי יונתן walk in a cemetery. רבי יונתן's תכלת drags on the ground. רבי חייא tells him to lift it so the dead will not feel insulted.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי חייא and רבי יונתן were walking in a cemetery. The blue string (תכלת) of רבי יונתן's ציצית was hanging down and dragging on the ground. רבי חייא said to him: 'Lift it up, so the dead will not say: Tomorrow they are coming to join us, and now they are mocking us!'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a story that shows the idea of not mocking the dead. רבי חייא tells his friend to lift his ציצית while walking among the graves.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Wearing ציצית in front of the dead looks like showing off a מצוה they can no longer do. That is exactly the 'לעג לרש' (mocking the poor) idea from Step 23. רבי חייא assumes the dead are aware of this and feel hurt. This assumption is what the next step will challenge.

keyTerms.meaning: The blue string (תכלת) of the ציצית

steps.whyThisMatters: This story is the source for the halacha that one should not walk among graves with exposed ציצית, so as not to mock the dead.

phrases.english: Rabbi Chiyya and Rabbi Yonatan
were walking along in a cemetery.
The blue string (of the tzitzis) of Rabbi Yonatan was hanging down (dragging).
phrases.notes: It was dragging over the graves.

phrases.english: Rabbi Chiyya said to him: Lift it up,
so that they (the dead) should not say:
Tomorrow they are coming to (join) us,
phrases.notes: Meaning: soon they too will die and be buried here.

phrases.english: and now they are insulting us.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי חִיָּיא וְרַבִּי יוֹנָתָן הֲווֹ שָׁקְלִי וְאָזְלִי בְּבֵית הַקְּבָרוֹת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the theme of honoring the dead and not mocking them ('לעג לרש') with a story.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Do not show off מצוות such as ציצית in front of the dead, because they feel mocked.

steps.title: Do the dead really know that much?
steps.stepSummary: רבי יונתן challenges רבי חייא from a פסוק in קהלת that says the dead know nothing.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יונתן said to him: 'Do the dead really know all this? Isn't it written: "And the dead know nothing"?'
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יונתן pushes back. He brings a פסוק that seems to say the dead have no awareness at all, so they could not feel insulted.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי חייא's instruction only makes sense if the dead are aware of what happens around them. The פסוק in קהלת (9:5) seems to state plainly that they are not. If so, there is no reason to lift the ציצית.

keyTerms.meaning: But isn't it written? (introduces a challenge from a פסוק)

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: וּמִי יָדְעִי כּוּלֵּי הַאי?
phrases.english: He (Rabbi Yonatan) said to him: Do they really know so much?
But isn't it written:
"And the dead know nothing"!

steps.triggerLanguage: וּמִי יָדְעִי כּוּלֵּי הַאי? וְהָא כְּתִיב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the assumption behind רבי חייא's instruction.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי חייא's assumption that the dead are aware and can feel insulted.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A פסוק explicitly says the dead know nothing, so they cannot be insulted.

steps.title: You did not learn the verse properly
steps.stepSummary: רבי חייא answers that רבי יונתן has not studied the פסוק carefully enough or had it explained properly.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי חייא said to him: 'If you read it, you did not read it a second time. If you read it a second time, you did not read it a third time. If you read it a third time, nobody explained it to you.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבי חייא starts his answer by telling רבי יונתן that he has misunderstood the פסוק. This line sets up the correct explanation that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי חייא does not deny the פסוק. He says its plain surface reading is wrong. This is a sharp way of saying that the real meaning needs deeper study and proper teaching.

keyTerms.meaning: You reviewed it a second time
You reviewed it a third time

steps.confusionAlert: Do not take 'שָׁנִיתָ' here to mean 'you learned משנה'. In this phrase it means 'you read it a second time', from the root meaning 'two'.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: אִם קָרִיתָ — לֹא שָׁנִיתָ.
phrases.english: He (Rabbi Chiyya) said to him: If you read it, you did not read it again.
If you read it a second time, you did not read it a third time.
If you read it a third time, they did not explain it to you (properly).

steps.triggerLanguage: אִם קָרִיתָ — לֹא שָׁנִיתָ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens the answer to רבי יונתן's challenge by rejecting his reading of the פסוק.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Rejection of the plain reading of the challenging פסוק, setting up a reinterpretation.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The פסוק plainly means that the dead have no awareness at all.
steps.terutzMaskana: The פסוק has a deeper meaning, which רבי חייא is about to explain.

steps.title: The 'living' in the verse are the righteous
steps.stepSummary: רבי חייא reinterprets the פסוק. 'The living' are the צדיקים, who are called living even after they die.
steps.simpleTranslation: '"For the living know that they will die": these are the צדיקים, who even in their death are called living.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבי חייא gives the real meaning of the פסוק. 'The living' means the צדיקים, who remain 'alive' even after death.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The words 'living' and 'dead' in the פסוק are not about physical life. The 'living' are צדיקים, who stay alive and aware even in death. By contrast, as the גמרא explains on the next amud, the 'dead' who 'know nothing' are the wicked, who are called dead even while alive. So the פסוק does not prove that all dead people are unaware.
steps.whatToRemember: צדיקים are called 'alive' even after death. Therefore the dead can be aware, and we must not mock them.

phrases.english: "For the living know that they will die":
phrases.notes: The first half of the same פסוק, קהלת 9:5.

phrases.english: these are the righteous,
who even in their death are called living,

steps.triggerLanguage: כִּי הַחַיִּים יוֹדְעִים שֶׁיָּמוּתוּ — אֵלּוּ צַדִּיקִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the correct explanation that Step 28 promised.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reinterpretation of the terms 'living' and 'dead' in the challenging פסוק.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'The dead' means everyone who has physically died.
steps.terutzMaskana: 'The living' are צדיקים, who are alive even in death. 'The dead know nothing' does not refer to them.

steps.title: Proof from the פסוק about בניהו בן יהוידע
steps.stepSummary: רבי חייא brings a פסוק describing בניהו בן יהוידע as 'בן איש חי', a 'living man'. This hints that צדיקים are called alive.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'As it says: "And בניהו בן יהוידע, son of a living (valiant) man, of many deeds, from קבצאל. He struck the two אריאל of מואב, and he went down and struck the lion inside the pit on a snowy day."'
steps.whatsHappening: רבי חייא brings a פסוק from שמואל ב (23:20) to support his claim that צדיקים are called 'living' even in death.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The key words are 'בן איש חי', literally 'a living man'. These words seem unnecessary, since everyone described is alive. So they must teach that a צדיק is called 'alive' even after death. The גמרא spells out this reading and the rest of the פסוק on the next amud.

keyTerms.meaning: As it is said (introduces a supporting פסוק)
בניהו בן יהוידע, one of דוד המלך's great warriors
A living man, or a valiant man

steps.confusionAlert: Only the words 'בן איש חי' are the actual proof. The rest of the פסוק (מואב, the lion, the snow) is quoted in full here and explained by the גמרא afterward.

phrases.english: As it is said:
"And Benayahu son of Yehoyada, son of a living (valiant) man,
phrases.notes: 'חי' (living) is the key word for the proof.

phrases.english: of many deeds, from Kabze'el,

phrases.aramaic: הוּא הִכָּה אֵת שְׁנֵי אֲרִאֵל מוֹאָב
phrases.english: he struck the two mighty altar-hearths of Moab,
and he went down and struck the lion
inside the pit on a snowy day."

steps.triggerLanguage: שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: וּבְנָיָהוּ בֶן יְהוֹיָדָע בֶּן אִישׁ חַי
